rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage echoes 41:49–51, where people persist in asking for good, despair when harmed, and withdraw after receiving mercy.
rows.anchor: The message in these verses is similar to that of 41:49–51

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also recalls descriptions of humanity as hasty in 21:37 and 17:11.
rows.anchor: This verse is similar to 21:37, Man was created of haste, and 17:11

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Here and in the parallel verses, man may mean humanity generally or disbelievers in particular.
rows.anchor: according to some, disbelievers in particular (Q, Ṭ).19

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Because the passage exempts those who pray, it suggests that the traits describe humanity broadly.
rows.anchor: the exception save those who perform prayer (v. 22) suggests that the broader interpretation is intended

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Hulūʿ combines greed and covetousness with severe anxiety.
rows.anchor: hulūʿ, which denotes greed and covetousness combined with severe anxiety

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Evil and good may mean misfortune and good fortune generally, or specifically illness and poverty versus health and wealth.
rows.anchor: evil and good can be understood as any form of misfortune or good fortune, respectively, or more specifically illness and poverty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jazūʿ conveys distress at misfortune and lack of forbearance, the opposite of the patience enjoined in 70:5.
rows.anchor: Fretful translates jazūʿ, which indicates both distress regarding one’s misfortune and a lack of forbearance

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: To overcome anxiety, recognize that circumstances come from God and be content with them.
rows.anchor: one should realize that the circumstances that give rise to them are from God and be content with them

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says health and wealth should be spent to seek gain in the Hereafter rather than this life.
rows.anchor: they should be expended for the sake of seeking gain in the Hereafter rather than gain in this life

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Those who possess the eight qualities in 70:22–35 are exempt from the blameworthy state described here.
rows.anchor: Those characterized by the eight qualities mentioned in the following verses (vv. 22–35) are then not subject to the blameworthy state

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: The begrudging fail to acknowledge God’s and others’ rights in their wealth and spend none of it in charity.
rows.anchor: fail to acknowledge the right that God and others have to it and thus fail to expend any of it in charity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like 23:1–11, this thorough list presents Islam’s moral and ritual duties; 23:3 adds turning away from idle talk, and 33:35 is another parallel.
rows.anchor: Similar to 23:1–11, which adds and who turn away from idle talk (23:3) to the list

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Constancy in prayer may mean performing the prescribed rites without neglect, as in 70:34, or simply praying all five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: perform the rites as prescribed without neglecting any aspect, as in v. 34, those who are mindful of their prayers

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The phrase may also mean maintaining prayer of the heart at all times.
rows.anchor: It may also indicate those who maintain the prayer of the heart at all times

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The acknowledged due in wealth primarily means obligatory zakāh, though some include voluntary charity beyond it.
rows.anchor: rather than supererogatory charity (Ṣadaqah; Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some interpreters hold that the acknowledged due includes charitable giving beyond obligatory alms.
rows.anchor: some maintain that it indicates charitable giving beyond the obligatory alms as well

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The beggar asks for help, while the deprived may need help but not ask; see also the discussion at 51:19.
rows.anchor: The beggar refers to those who request, while the deprived may refer to those who have need but do not ask

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list of people entitled to a share of one’s wealth is also given in 2:177.
rows.anchor: For a list of those who have an acknowledged due, or the right, to a share of one’s wealth, see 2:177

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affirming Judgment means believing in resurrection and the weighing of deeds, and living for the Hereafter rather than this world.
rows.anchor: belief in the Resurrection and the weighing of deeds and therefore leading a life focused on the Hereafter rather than this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of punishment may extend the duty to believe in Judgment or constitute a fourth duty: fearing the consequences of neglected obligations and disobedience.
rows.anchor: could be considered an extension of the third responsibility or as a fourth responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no security from punishment because it is inescapable.
rows.anchor: There is no security from the punishment, because it is inescapable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fifth duty is refraining from illicit sex; these verses repeat 23:5–7, and “those whom their right hands possess” means slave women with whom men have sex.
rows.anchor: Whom their right hands possess refers to slave women with whom one has sexual relations

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith promises Paradise to whoever guards what is between the jaws and legs.
rows.anchor: Whosoever is able to guarantee what is between his jawbones and what is between his legs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another hadith identifies the spread of illicit intercourse as an end-time sign.
rows.anchor: Another ḥadīth cites the spread of illicit sexual intercourse as one of the signs of the end of time

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Keeping trusts and pacts includes humanity’s primordial covenant with God and commitments to people, covering religion and worldly affairs.
rows.anchor: all of humanity is said to have made an initial pretemporal covenant or pact

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Upholding testimony may mean bearing witness to God’s Oneness and the other articles of faith.
rows.anchor: The seventh responsibility, which follows from maintaining trusts, is to testify to God’s Oneness

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another interpretation is testifying to God’s edicts and remaining true to them.
rows.anchor: this verse indicates testifying to God’s edicts and remaining true to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Testimony also means speaking truthfully in all matters, even against one’s kin, as developed in 2:283 and 4:135.
rows.anchor: testifying to the truth in all matters, even if it is against one’s kin

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith names three signs of hypocrisy: lying when speaking, breaking promises, and betraying a trust.
rows.anchor: The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies; when he makes a promise, he breaks

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Mindfulness means praying at the right time and observing necessary and recommended elements, including presence of heart.
rows.anchor: careful to pray at the right time and to maintain all of the necessary and recommended aspects of prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list begins and ends with prayer, showing prayer’s central place among religious acts.
rows.anchor: the manner in which this extended pericope on the responsibilities of Islam begins with prayer in vv. 22–23 and ends with prayer in this verse

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet urges establishing prayer without falling short and calls it the best deed.
rows.anchor: Establish [the prayer] and do not fall short. And know that the best of your deeds is prayer

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have said that prayer is his comfort.
rows.anchor: My comfort is in prayer

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The first matter for which a person is taken to account is prayer, meaning failure to pray.
rows.anchor: The first thing for which one will be taken to account is prayer

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One reading takes constancy as observing appointed prayer times and mindfulness as attention to every detail, from time and direction to purification and presence.
rows.anchor: those who are constant in their prayers (v. 23) refers to those who always observe the appointed times for prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of honored Gardens parallels the conclusion to the similar passage in 23:10–11.
rows.anchor: This promise is similar to that given at the end of the almost identical pericope in 23:10–11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The late Makkan surah takes its name from the jinn in verse 1 and the report that they heard the Quran, recognized revelation, and embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: a group of jinn who heard the Prophet’s recitation of the Quran, recognized it as Divine Revelation, and embraced Islam

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The surah connects Muhammad’s trials as the last Messenger to Noah’s trials; Noah is widely viewed as the first messenger, though earlier prophets such as Adam had less universal roles.
rows.anchor: the travails of Noah, widely regarded as the first messenger (Āl), although he had been preceded by other prophets

rows.speaker: Āl, Sy
rows.claim: Some commentators connect the abundant water promised to Quraysh with the rain promised to Noah’s people.
rows.anchor: the mention of the abundant rains promised to Noah’s people in 71:11 and the abundant water promised to the Quraysh in 72:16

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is placed amid the Prophet’s hardship in 619, after Abū Ṭālib’s death, his rejection at Ṭāʾif, and his search for protection.
rows.anchor: revealed at a time of great difficulty for the Prophet, in the year 619, when he had lost the protection of his uncle Abū Ṭālib

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Ṭāʾif mob, Muhammad and Zayd ibn Ḥārith sought refuge in an orchard; the Prophet prayed, and Salmān al-Fārsī helped him escape and later became a close Companion.
rows.anchor: The Prophet and Zayd ibn Ḥārith (d. 629), who had traveled with him, sought refuge in an orchard

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: At Nakhlah, while the Prophet prayed and recited Sūrah 55 according to some, seven or nine jinn listened and converted to Islam.
rows.anchor: Some say that he was reciting al-Raḥmān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This account presents the surah as divine solace: despite the Prophet’s trials, his message was heard and his mission spread.
rows.anchor: this sūrah is seen as a gift of solace from God, letting the Prophet know that, despite his trials

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says the jinn were distressed after losing access to heavenly messages, searched for the cause, heard the Quran at morning prayer, and told their people it had blocked those reports.
rows.anchor: A group of them came upon the Prophet while he was leading his Companions in the morning prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heaven and earth are both literal and symbolic: physical ascent symbolizes movement toward God, while heaven also signifies higher ontological planes.
rows.anchor: “up”is the reality in physical space that best symbolizes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn are unseen psychic beings between the material and spiritual realms; they also inhabit earth, which some say they occupied before humanity.
rows.anchor: The jinn, as psychic beings unseen to most human beings, occupy an intermediate state between the material realm of our physical experiences and the angelic and spiritual realms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn are said to overhear angels, foretell events, and grant special powers, but knowledge from them has no spiritual value and differs from divine or angelic inspiration.
rows.anchor: The jinn are said to have the ability to“eavesdrop” on angelic communications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet has no power beyond faithfully delivering God’s message, a recurring Quranic theme.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is being told to deny that he has any power beyond that of delivering God’s message faithfully

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs tended toward idol worship, the Quran repeatedly rejects taking prophets or angels as lords, as in 3:79–80.
rows.anchor: Given the tendency of the Arabs toward idol worship, this theme recurs throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: Āl, IK
rows.claim: Al-Muzzammil is among the earliest Makkan surahs; many commentators date verse 20 about a year after the rest, while others consider it Madinan.
rows.anchor: Many commentators maintain that v. 20 was revealed about one year later than the remainder of the sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl, JJ
rows.claim: Others hold that verse 20 comes from the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: others believe that v. 20 is from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All verses except 20 are said to have been revealed immediately after the first five verses of Sūrah 74.
rows.anchor: all of the verses except v. 20 are said to have been revealed immediately after the first five verses of Sūrah 74

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is named for God’s address to the Prophet as “thou enwrapped.”
rows.anchor: This sūrah takes its name from God’s addressing the Prophet as thou enwrapped

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Night vigil was obligatory before the five daily prayers were established, but the final verse later made it voluntary.
rows.anchor: which was made obligatory before the five daily prayers had been established

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The address about the weighty Word follows the previous surah’s messengers, all of whom received a weighty Word in some form.
rows.anchor: The direct address to the Prophet, which tells him of the weighty Word (v. 5) of revelation, follows upon the mention of the messengers in the last verses of the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–9 establish night vigil and its obligation; 10–14 counsel patience toward rejecters; 15–19 compare Muhammad with Moses and evoke Judgment; verse 20 removes the obligation while retaining prayer and alms.
rows.anchor: The first section (vv. 1–9) establishes the supremacy of night vigil and the obligation to perform it

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Choking food may include Zaqqūm, a vile thorn, inedible filth, and fiery thorns that cannot be vomited or swallowed; alternatively, these may collectively describe the food.
rows.anchor: including the tree of Zaqqūm (44:43; cf. 37:62; 56:52), a vile thorn (88:6), filth, which none eat

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Some commentators consider the whole surah Makkan, while others assign its final section, verses 31–56, to the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: according to some commentators, Makkan in its entirety (Bg), but others maintain that the last section (vv. 31–56) is from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah continues the previous one’s account of the Prophet covering himself at the onset of revelation, then stresses his role as warner.
rows.anchor: both are said to respond to the Prophet’s covering himself when the experience of the revelation began

rows.speaker: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh
rows.claim: The Prophet recounts that after a month at Mt. Ḥirāʾ he saw Gabriel between heaven and earth, fell in fear, asked to be covered, and received 74:1–5.
rows.anchor: I passed a month at Mt. Ḥirāʾ, and when my stay came to an end, I came down.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify 96:1–5 as the Quran’s first revelation, while the cited account assigns that status to 74:1–5.
rows.anchor: Although most commentators agree that 96:1–5 constitutes the first revelation of the Quran

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: The reference to the same angel means the narration concerns a second revelation experience, making these verses the first revelation after 96:1–5.
rows.anchor: the reference to “the same angel who came to me in the cave of Ḥirāʾ” indicates that this narration pertains to the second experience of the revelation

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the account marks the first command to warn and become a Messenger, whereas 96:1–5 began revelation as a whole.
rows.anchor: this account provides the first command to warn, thus to go forth as a Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–7 exhort the Prophet, 8–10 introduce Judgment, 11–25 polemicize against deniers of Muhammad’s prophethood, and 26–31 evoke their punishment.
rows.anchor: vv.8–10 warn of the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: Āl, Ṭ
rows.claim: “Nay” rejects claims that people can know God’s hosts’ number or overcome them; the oath also recalls other oaths on the moon and the night-day alternation.
rows.anchor: Nay! expresses a rejection of those who suppose that they can know the number of God’s hosts or that they can overcome them

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The phrase may refer to Saqar, which is one of the greatest calamities, or to the denial of Muhammad’s prophethood as a great sin.
rows.anchor: Here it refers to Saqar (Q, Ṭ), meaning that Saqar is one of the greatest calamities

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Some infer from “one of the calamities” that calamities of this kind will be endless.
rows.anchor: Some understand the assertion that it is only one of the calamities to mean that such calamities will be endless

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another reading takes the phrase as the disbelievers’ denial of Muhammad’s prophethood, one of the greatest sins.
rows.anchor: It could also refer to the disbelievers’ denial of the prophethood of Muhammad, meaning that such denial is one of the greatest sins

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some exegetes attach verse 36 grammatically to the command in verses 1–2: the Prophet is to rise and warn humanity.
rows.anchor: v. 36 may be a distant adverbial clause that continues the command in vv. 1–2

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most relate it to verse 35, so Saqar’s gravity itself serves as a warning.
rows.anchor: Most, however, view it in relation to the previous verse, indicating that the gravity of Saqar should serve as a warner

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: In context, “warner” may be an Attribute of God or refer to the Quran.
rows.anchor: warner may also be viewed as an Attribute of God or a reference to the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qiyāmah is an early Makkan surah named for the Resurrection oath in verse 1 and is also called Lā uqsimu, after the opening of verses 1–2.
rows.anchor: an early Makkan sūrah that takes its name from God’s swearing by the Resurrection in the first verse

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The surah’s opening contains two oaths, and the second has many interpretations.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with two oaths (vv. 1–2), the second of which is subject to much interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah rebukes Resurrection deniers and describes its signs, counsels patience in receiving revelation, contrasts the final ends of believers and disbelievers, and closes with life’s stages as proof of resurrection.
rows.anchor: It then rebukes those who deny the Day of Resurrection and speaks of its signs (vv. 3–15)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 13 echoes 82:5; what people sent ahead may mean all their deeds or only good deeds that testify for them and earn reward.
rows.anchor: That which he has sent forth refers either to all of the deeds that individuals have performed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What a person leaves behind may mean good deeds not done in life or good deeds that continue to bear fruit.
rows.anchor: That which he has left behind refers either to the good deeds that were not performed in this life or to the good deeds that continue to bear fruit

rows.speaker: a famous ḥadīth
rows.claim: A person who establishes a good practice receives its own reward and an equal reward for later followers; one who establishes an evil practice bears its burden and theirs.
rows.anchor: And whosoever establishes a bad custom

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Most scholars place the surah in Madinah; others place all but verse 24 there, verses 23–31 in Makkah, or the whole surah in Makkah.
rows.anchor: A minority maintain that the entire sūrah was revealed in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its title from the mention of man in its first verse.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its title from the mention of man in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its other names are Hal atā (“Has There Not Come”), al-Dahr (“Endless Time”), and al-Abrār (“The Pious”), named for its opening and the pious’ reward in verses 5–22.
rows.anchor: Another name is al-Abrār, “The Pious,” for its discussion of the rewards due to the pious in vv. 5–22

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly often recited this surah with Sūrah 32 during Friday dawn prayer.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet would often recite this sūrah along with Sūrah 32, al-Sajdah, during the early morning prayer

rows.speaker: most Shiite and some Sunni sources
rows.claim: These verses are associated with ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, Ḥasan, and Ḥusayn; the account says illness prompted a vow to fast and donate food to a needy person, orphan, and captive.
rows.anchor: According to most Shiite and some Sunni sources, vv. 5–22 were revealed in relation to the family of the Prophet

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī
rows.claim: In the reported occasion, ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, and their helper Fizzah vow to fast three days if the sick sons recover, then give their food to an indigent person, an orphan, and a captive.
rows.anchor: So ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, and Fizzah, their house helper, vowed that if Ḥasan and Ḥusayn recovered, they would fast for three days

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: According to some accounts, Ḥasan and Ḥusayn also made the vow.
rows.anchor: according to some, Ḥasan and Ḥusayn made the same vow

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the family gave away food for three nights, the Prophet saw their suffering and Gabriel descended, telling Muhammad to receive this surah as congratulations on his family.
rows.anchor: God congratulates you for having such a family

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In verses 1–2, man may refer to Adam, all humanity, or both.
rows.anchor: refers to Adam, all of humanity (R), or both

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: As a rhetorical question, the verse may mean that human beings have never been unknown to God.
rows.anchor: indicating that there has never been a time when human beings were not known to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the rhetorical question emphasizes that humanity once did not exist.
rows.anchor: emphasizing that there was indeed a time when man was a thing unknown, meaning nonexistent

rows.speaker: JJ, Q, R, Ṭs
rows.claim: With the alternative translation “There has come upon man,” most interpreters mean the period when Adam was not yet fully formed.
rows.anchor: which is taken by most as a reference to the time when Adam was not yet fully formed

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The alternative translation may instead refer broadly to the time before humanity existed.
rows.anchor: or more generally to the time when humanity had not yet come into existence

rows.speaker: Aj, JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The verses may enjoin naming God in the daily prayers; Aj also reads them as remembrance of God at every moment.
rows.anchor: These verses enjoin mentioning the Name of God during the daily prayers

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: In context, the command counsels remembering God amid worldly tribulations; many Sufis take verse 25 as invoking God’s Supreme Name, Allāh.
rows.anchor: many Sufis take v. 25 as an injunction to invoke the Supreme Divine Name, Allāh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Glorifying God at length by night enjoins voluntary night vigil and prayer, with related passages elsewhere and in 73:2, 6, and 20.
rows.anchor: Glorify Him by night at length enjoins the supererogatory practice of night vigil and prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This late Makkan surah is named for the Great Tiding in verse 2, understood by most as the Quran or Resurrection; it is also called al-Muʿṣirāt and al-Tasāʾul for its rain-cloud and questioning themes.
rows.anchor: a late Makkan sūrah, takes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening questions concern disbelief in the Resurrection, the revelation of the Quran, or both; Ibn ʿAjībah links a Resurrection reading to the previous surah’s Day of Division.
rows.anchor: Insofar as the Great Tiding refers to the Resurrection, this sūrah is connected to the previous sūrah’s discussion of the Day of Division

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: If the Great Tiding means the Quran, this surah follows directly from the previous surah’s last verse.
rows.anchor: Insofar as the Great Tiding refers to the Quran, this sūrah follows directly upon the last verse of the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–5 describe deniers, 6–16 point to creation as evidence, and 17–40 depict the Resurrection, the Day of Division, and the differing return of believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Rather than argue against their disbelief, vv. 6–16 point to all of those things that God has created as signs
